items.followUp: Write three differences between the atomic models of Thomson and Rutherford.

rubric.why: Checks the difference between the electron energy levels in the two models.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s unspecified electron energy levels with Bohr’s definite energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for stating that Rutherford’s model did not specify fixed energy levels, whereas Bohr’s model did.

rubric.why: Checks the difference in the orbits allowed for electrons.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model did not restrict electrons to particular orbits, whereas Bohr proposed permitted fixed orbits.
rubric.how: Award for a valid contrast between unrestricted orbits and Bohr’s permitted orbits.

rubric.why: Checks the predicted energy behaviour of orbiting electrons.
rubric.description: Contrasts the energy radiation predicted for Rutherford’s orbiting electrons with Bohr’s non-radiating stationary orbits.
rubric.how: Award for describing energy loss or radiation in Rutherford’s model and no radiation in Bohr’s stationary orbits.

rubric.why: Checks how the models account for atomic stability.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability, while Bohr’s model accounted for it.
rubric.how: Award for the correct contrast about stability.

rubric.why: Checks the models’ explanations of atomic spectra.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s inability to explain the hydrogen line spectrum with Bohr’s explanation of it.
rubric.how: Award for identifying Bohr’s explanation of the hydrogen line spectrum and Rutherford’s failure to explain it.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model did not assign electrons fixed energy levels; Bohr’s model gave electrons definite energy levels.
Rutherford’s model did not restrict electrons to particular orbits; Bohr’s model allowed only permitted orbits.
According to Rutherford’s model, orbiting electrons would radiate energy and lose it continuously; Bohr’s electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.
Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom; Bohr’s model explained atomic stability.
Rutherford’s model could not explain the hydrogen line spectrum; Bohr’s model explained it.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and explain how temperature and intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid.
rubric.how: Award for including vapour pressure, the vapour, and equilibrium with the liquid.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction of change.

rubric.why: Checks how the nature of the liquid affects vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States that more volatile liquids, with weaker intermolecular attractions, have higher vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award for a correct relationship between volatility or intermolecular attractions and vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Distinguishes equilibrium vapour pressure from the rate of reaching equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that surface area does not change equilibrium vapour pressure at a fixed temperature, though it can affect how quickly equilibrium is reached.
rubric.how: Award for this distinction; do not award for claiming that surface area changes the equilibrium vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour when it is in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
As temperature increases, vapour pressure increases.
More volatile liquids, which have weaker intermolecular attractions, have higher vapour pressure.
At a fixed temperature, surface area does not affect equilibrium vapour pressure; it only changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached.
